χ2superscript𝜒2\chi^{2}

Handcrafted global descriptors usually used a single descriptor to describe the entire point cloud. According to the type of space division, they could be divided into BEV-based, discretization-based, and point-based methods. Three representative methods were shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").

BEV projection gained significant attention in the robotics community due to its ability to enhance algorithm efficiency through dimension reduction, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Scan Context (SC)[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] family and pairwise matching were two mainstream methods.

SC Family. As illustrated in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), the pioneering work SC[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] partitioned the horizontal space into discrete bins while maintaining the points’ maximum height to generate a 2D matrix descriptor. It utilized the ring key to search for potential matches and conducted a column-wise comparison to identify the closest one. This method demonstrated promising performance but might fail when dealing with significant lateral offsets. Subsequently, researchers proposed a series of SC-based variant methods, which employed the polar and cart context[[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7)], intensities[[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)], frequency domain[[144](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib144)], local reference frame (LRF)[[139](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib139)], F-norm [[143](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib143)], and spatial binary pattern (SBP) [[145](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib145)] to enhance performance. Furthermore, certain studies [[175](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib175), [176](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib176), [177](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib177)] had incorporated SC-based methods into the LCD module of LiDAR SLAM frameworks to enhance the performance of localization and map construction.

Pairwise Matching. LiDAR Iris[[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib47)] drew inspiration from human iris signatures, utilizing LoG-Gabor filtering and thresholding to create binary signature images, then measuring descriptor similarities using Hamming distance. Some methods also employed weighted distances[[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib67)] and orientation-invariant metrics[[141](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib141), [142](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib142)] for pairwise similarity computation.
The discretization processing transformed the point cloud into 3D discrete representations, categorized into fixed and unfixed size-based approaches.

Fixed-size Discretization. Magnussonet al.[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146)] mapped the point cloud to normal distribution transform (NDT) voxels and created a histogram based on the probability density function of the local surface. They calculated the descriptor similarities using weighted Euclidean distances. This method demonstrated the potential of NDT descriptors for place recognition. Subsequently, researchers introduced techniques like k-means++ clustering[[178](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib178)] and normalized cross-correlation metrics[[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [179](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib179)] to enhance generalization. Cao et al.[[148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] also generated a numerical descriptor by detecting contours and computing spectrum energies from wedge-shaped voxels.

Unfixed-size Discretization. As depicted in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), DELIGHT [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib64), [147](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib147)] divided the support region into two concentric spheres and got non-overlapping bins by horizontal and azimuthal divisions. It computed intensity histograms for each bin and assessed descriptor similarities by chi-squared tests. Notably, the descriptor could be local or global based on the descriptor’s radius and center point.

Several methods treated place recognition as a histogram matching problem, encoding angle[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62)] and height[[48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48)] information and calculating histogram similarities using Wasserstein metric[[48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48)], Sørensen[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62)], and χ2superscript𝜒2\chi^{2} distances[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62)]. They achieved rotation invariance and overcame noises. As shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), a parallel track of works followed a projection-based scheme. M2DP[[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149)] and C-M2DP[[150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] projected the point cloud onto multiple 2D planes using azimuth and elevation angles, counting point density attributes to create the descriptor. Computing multi-view density signatures enabled accurate descriptions with fewer computational resources, making it particularly effective for sparse point clouds.
χ2superscript𝜒2\chi^{2}

This section explored learning-based methods for obtaining global descriptors, categorized into five groups based on network architecture and model mechanism: point-based, discretization-based, classification-based, projection-based, and fusion-based methods.

One prevalent approach directly utilized the inherent 3D spatial information for LiDAR point cloud processing, involving point-wise MLP, point convolution, and graph representation, as shown in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").

Pointwise MLP. The pioneering end-to-end work PointNetVLAD [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12)] combined PointNet [[117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib117)] for local feature extraction and NetVLAD[[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib43)] for global descriptor generation. It employed metric learning [[180](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib180)] and introduced the lazy triplet and quadruplet loss functions to enhance the generality of global descriptors. Afterward, PCAN[[70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70)] and SOE-Net[[151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151)] improved high-dimensional feature representation by incorporating attention mechanisms. As depicted in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), LCD-Net[[152](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib152)] utilized the PointVoxel-RCNN (PV-RCNN)[[181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib181)] architecture and combined the feature extraction capabilities of deep neural network with transport theory algorithms.

Point Convolution. DH3D[[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71)] introduced a Siamese network for local feature detection, description, and global descriptor extraction in a single forward pass. It incorporated multi-level spatial contextual information and channel-wise feature correlations using flex convolution (FlexConv)[[182](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib182)] and squeeze-and-excitation (SE)[[183](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib183)]. As shown in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), EPC-Net[[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib69)] was a compact model based on edge convolution, simplifying the process with spatial-adjacent matrices and proxy points. It achieved excellent performance while significantly reducing computational memory.

Graph Representation. Graph networks efficiently capture underlying geometric and shape properties, allowing for effective processing and feature comparison across multiple locations within graphs. As illustrated in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), LPD-Net[[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5)] and vLPD-Net[[154](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib154)] combined adaptive local feature extraction with a graph-based neighborhood aggregation module. They extracted multiple local features, including curvature, height, and density, and employed a graph neural network (GNN) for feature aggregation. Several works integrated an attention module to discern task-relevant features[[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13)], learn spatial relationships between regions[[155](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib155)], and mitigate the influence of movable noises[[153](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib153)].
We divided discretization-based methods into sparse and dense representations based on voxel density.
Sparse Representation. Three approaches for generating global descriptors using 3D CNNs on sparse volume representations were feature pyramid network (FPN), transformer network, and other methods.

*1) FPN*. MinkLoc3D[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156)], a pioneering work based on sparse voxelization, employed a 3D FPN[[184](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib184)] architecture and generalized-mean (GeM)[[185](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib185)] pooling for global descriptor generation. It showcased a simple and elegant architecture, highlighting the potential of sparse voxelized representation and sparse convolutions for efficient 3D feature extraction. Later works extended MinkLoc3D[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156)] by incorporating intensity[[161](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib161)], image[[157](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib157)], and attention[[158](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib158), [160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib160)] to enhance recognition performance.

*2) Transformer Network*. TransLoc3D[[159](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib159)] re-weighted features from multiple receptive scales using an attention map and incorporated external attention layers for capturing long-range contextual information. SVT-Net[[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib8)], illustrated in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.2 Discretization-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), introduced two types of transformers to capture short-range local features and long-range contextual features, respectively. Despite a shallow network architecture, it generated descriptive descriptors.

*3) Other Methods*. LoGG3D-Net[[162](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib162)] utilized sparse U-Net[[186](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib186)] for high-dimensional feature embedding and introduced a local consistency loss for feature similarity maximization. It exhibited superior end-to-end performance, operating in near real-time.
Dense Representation. Likewise, we broadly categorized dense representation-based approaches into transformer network, DNN, and other methods.

*1) Transformer Network*. HiTPR [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165)] utilized a short-range transformer to extract local features within cells and a long-range transformer to encode global relations among the cells. It enhanced the relevance of local neighbors and global contextual dependencies, showcasing its superior effectiveness. As shown in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.2 Discretization-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), NDT-Transformer[[166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166)] introduced a novel network with three stacked transformer encoders, learning a global descriptor from discrete NDT cells. It struck a valuable balance between state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance and runtime, making it a valuable addition to NDT-based SLAM and MCL methods.

*2) DNN*. SpoxelNet[[163](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib163)] voxelized the point cloud in spherical coordinates, representing voxel occupancy using ternary values. It extracted multi-scale structural features and generated a global descriptor by concatenating features from various directions. This method effectively handled occlusion and moving objects in crowded indoor spaces.

*3) Other Methods*. Voxel-based representation learning (VBRL)[[164](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib164)] tackled long-term place recognition by jointly learning voxel importance and feature modalities using structured sparsity-inducing norms. It integrated all features into a unified regularized optimization formulation.

Several approaches addressed the place recognition problem using classifiers. FastLCD [[65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65)] encoded multi-modality features into a global descriptor, detecting candidate loop closures using supervised learning and rejecting false positives through cross-validation and post-verification. On the other hand, Habich et al.[[187](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib187)] used a compact global descriptor[[188](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib188)] to encode each LiDAR scan, performed loop searches within a variable radius based on the largest eigenvalue of the position covariance matrix and predicted loop events using an AdaBoost[[189](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib189)] classifier.

Following the taxonomy of learning-based 2D local descriptors (Section [3.1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S3.SS1.SSS2 "3.1.2 2D-based Methods ‣ 3.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 3 LPR Techniques: Local Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")), this section also categorized projection methods into spherical view and BEV.
Spherical View. Using spherical projection images as input, three representative methods included siamese network, transformer network, and 2D CNN only.

*1) Siamese Network*. Yin et al.[[167](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib167)] transformed the point cloud into a one-channel image using range distribution and spherical coordinates. They used a Siamese CNN to convert LCD into a similarity modeling problem, improving search efficiency by combining Euclidean metric and kd-tree. MMCS-Net[[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168)] incorporated a Siamese CNN with shallow-deep feature fusion and a cascaded attention mechanism to handle pseudo images. It effectively encoded targeted features for challenging scenes, striking a favorable balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

*2) Transformer Network*. SeqOT[[169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169)] employed multi-scale transformers to generate sub-descriptors that fuse spatial and temporal information from sequential LiDAR range images. The yaw-rotation-invariant architecture ensured robustness to viewpoint changes and scan order, enabling reliable place recognition even in opposite directions. As depicted in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2.4 Projection-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), OverlapTransformer[[170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170)] applied a modified OverlapNetLeg to extract features from range images and integrated a transformer module to capture relative feature locations and global information. It demonstrated fast running speed and robust generalization across diverse environments. Attention-based deep learning network (AttDLNet)[[171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] also incorporated a four-layer attention network to capture long-range context and inter-feature relationships.

*3) 2D CNN Only*. OREOS[[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50)] used 2D convolutional and max pooling layers to extract features from 2D range images, enhancing the descriptor performance via a triple loss function and strong negative mining strategy. It efficiently computed the descriptor while enabling long-term 3-DoF metric localization in outdoor environments.
BEV. Two representative BEV-based methods were encoder-decoder network and 2D CNN only.

*1) Encoder-Decoder Network*. As shown in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2.4 Projection-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), differentiable scan context with orientation (DiSCO)[[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68)] employed an encoder-decoder network to extract descriptors and estimated relative orientation through Fourier-Mellin Transform and differentiable phase correlation. It enhanced the interpretability and efficiency of the feature extractor.

*2) 2D CNN Only*. Scan context image (SCI)[[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)] extended SC[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] into three channels, enabling robot localization on a grid map through a convolutional neural network-based place classification. It demonstrated robust year-round localization with only a single day of learning.

These methods combined LiDAR and image features to enhance descriptor capabilities. Several works transformed the point cloud into an image and only utilized a 2D network for descriptor extraction. CORAL[[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18)] used ResNet18[[190](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib190)] to extract multi-scale features from elevation and visual images. Bernreiteret al.[[173](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib173)] employed spherical CNNs[[191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib191), [192](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib192), [193](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib193)] to learn a multi-modal descriptor from spherical and visual images. As depicted in Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.2.5 Fusion-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey"), another line of research involved employing both 2D and 3D networks. Adafusion[[174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174)] and PIC-Net[[172](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib172)] incorporated an attention mechanism to learn adaptive feature weights and created a compound descriptor using two types of networks.

Global descriptors were currently the most popular place recognition method, which could provide information about the entire scene, unaffected by local changes. The progress of deep learning in 3D computer vision paved the way for data-driven methods in LPR. Several observations were summarized as follows:
For the handcrafted part:

* • BEV[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)] demonstrated superior performance in flat structural environments but has three main limitations: (1) When the z-axis of the LiDAR changed in the global coordinate system, poor results might arise because these methods assumed local planar vehicle motion. (2) Large lateral offsets might cause missed loops or failed re-localization. (3) Rotation matching could only compute yaw angles, leading to potential local optimum issues if used as initial poses for iterative closest point (ICP)[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)]. * • Discretization-based methods[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146), [84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] could describe the local surface using robust mathematical theories. However, increasing the resolution would significantly incur a heavy computational burden. * • Point-based methods[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] were the most basic global descriptor methods. However, they required expensive neighbor searching to establish topological relationships. Furthermore, projection operations [[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] might result in information loss and cause potential false positives.

BEV[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)] demonstrated superior performance in flat structural environments but has three main limitations: (1) When the z-axis of the LiDAR changed in the global coordinate system, poor results might arise because these methods assumed local planar vehicle motion. (2) Large lateral offsets might cause missed loops or failed re-localization. (3) Rotation matching could only compute yaw angles, leading to potential local optimum issues if used as initial poses for iterative closest point (ICP)[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)].

Discretization-based methods[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146), [84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] could describe the local surface using robust mathematical theories. However, increasing the resolution would significantly incur a heavy computational burden.

Point-based methods[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] were the most basic global descriptor methods. However, they required expensive neighbor searching to establish topological relationships. Furthermore, projection operations [[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] might result in information loss and cause potential false positives.
For the learning part:

* • Learning-based methods delivered impressive efficiency and accurate recognition but heavily relied on ample training samples and extensive data cleaning. Real-world environments presented additional challenges, including noise, occlusions, and uncertainties in LiDAR measurements. Consequently, transfer learning might be necessary for specific applications. * • Transformers [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166), [169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] excelled at capturing long-range dependencies and contextual relationships, enabling reliable recognition in cluttered environments. However, their substantial computational demands constrained the batch size for metric learning. * • Sparse convolutional architectures[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156), [161](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib161), [157](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib157), [160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib160)] excelled at generating informative local features while struggling to discriminate feature size in dynamic scenarios. Additionally, simply stacking convolution layers might neglect long-range contextual information. * • Point-based methods [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70), [151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151), [71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13)] were permutation invariant and could handle unordered point clouds but lacked explicit capture of local spatial relationships. Classification-based methods [[65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65), [187](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib187)] assigned higher weights to informative features during training, emphasizing discriminative features. However, the specific contribution of each weak classifier to the overall prediction might be less interpretable. * • Projection-based methods[[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)] had lower computational complexity and offered more interpretable results. However, they might suffer from information loss due to dimensionality reduction. Fusion-based methods[[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18), [174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174), [173](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib173)] harnessed the complementary strengths of different sensors. Nevertheless, achieving consistent data association in dynamic environments remained challenging.

Learning-based methods delivered impressive efficiency and accurate recognition but heavily relied on ample training samples and extensive data cleaning. Real-world environments presented additional challenges, including noise, occlusions, and uncertainties in LiDAR measurements. Consequently, transfer learning might be necessary for specific applications.

Transformers [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166), [169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] excelled at capturing long-range dependencies and contextual relationships, enabling reliable recognition in cluttered environments. However, their substantial computational demands constrained the batch size for metric learning.

Sparse convolutional architectures[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156), [161](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib161), [157](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib157), [160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib160)] excelled at generating informative local features while struggling to discriminate feature size in dynamic scenarios. Additionally, simply stacking convolution layers might neglect long-range contextual information.

Point-based methods [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70), [151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151), [71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13)] were permutation invariant and could handle unordered point clouds but lacked explicit capture of local spatial relationships. Classification-based methods [[65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65), [187](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib187)] assigned higher weights to informative features during training, emphasizing discriminative features. However, the specific contribution of each weak classifier to the overall prediction might be less interpretable.

Projection-based methods[[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)] had lower computational complexity and offered more interpretable results. However, they might suffer from information loss due to dimensionality reduction. Fusion-based methods[[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18), [174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174), [173](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib173)] harnessed the complementary strengths of different sensors. Nevertheless, achieving consistent data association in dynamic environments remained challenging.

Segments are meaningful region divisions characterized by similar geometric properties. These methods divide the point cloud into segments and three representative methods are shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").
These approaches generally extracted segment features for place recognition and could be divided into matching-based and similarity-based methods.
Segment-based matching for finding correspondences primarily comprised the SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] family and other methods.

SegMatch Family. The pioneering work SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)], depicted in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), employed Euclidean clustering to partition the point cloud into segments and extracted eigenvalue-based features. It effectively identified potential correspondences using random forest and random sample consensus (RANSAC)[[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)]-based geometric verification. Dubé et al.[[198](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib198)] enhanced SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] by tracking a single segment using region-growing-based incremental segmentation. Moreover, certain studies effectively integrated SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] into traditional LiDAR SLAM[[199](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib199)] and multi-robot systems [[200](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib200)].

Other Methods. DL-SLAM [[201](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib201)] employed k-means to extract segments from a 2.5D heightmap and defined five descriptors to facilitate segment matching. RDC-SLAM[[202](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib202)] combined an eigenvalue-based segment descriptor, k nearest neighbors (KNN) search, and RANSAC-based verification[[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)] to refine relative poses. It accurately fused information from multiple robots without prior knowledge. Gong et al.[[203](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib203)] constructed a spatial relation graph to represent segments, effectively capturing general spatial relations between irregular clusters.

Seed [[204](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib204)] developed a segmentation-based egocentric descriptor, incorporating topological information into SC-based place recognition[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)]. It achieved translation and rotation invariance by utilizing the inner topological structure of segmented objects.
Neural network application on segments primarily involved matching, classification, and similarity computation.

Tinchev et al.[[205](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib205)] encoded geometric properties and point distribution of segments to extract repeatable oriented key poses, which were matched using reliable shape descriptors and a Random Forest. However, significant changes in the sensor’s vantage point could negatively impact segment-matching performance. Tinchev et al.[[206](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib206)] utilized convolution[[207](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib207)] to obtain an embedding space suitable for urban and natural scenarios. They subsequently estimated match quality through probabilistic geometric validation.

Several works computed the category of segments by performing classification in the descriptor space. categorized into SegMap[[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208)] family and other methods.

*1) SegMap Family*. As shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), the pioneering work SegMap[[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208)] incrementally clustered point clouds to create a global segment map. It employed segment-wise KNN retrieval with a data-driven descriptor extractor comprising three convolutional and two fully connected layers, then assigned a classification score using a fully connected network. It enabled high compression rates in environment reconstruction and facilitated large-scale 3D LiDAR SLAM. Subsequently, researchers successfully integrated SegMap [[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195)] into LiDAR SLAM[[209](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib209)] and segment-based mapping framework[[210](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib210)].

*2) Other Methods*. Wietrzykowski et al.[[211](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib211)] proposed a DNN that improved segment-based descriptors by learning visual context from synthetic LiDAR intensity images. They claimed that using the latest LiDAR and ambient images could yield additional performance improvements. OneShot[[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib66)] employed a range image-based method[[212](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib212)] for segment extraction and a custom-tailored neural network to extract LiDAR-Vision descriptors.

Another approach constructed segment-based descriptors and assessed their similarities, thus combining the advantages of segments and global descriptors. Deep scan context (DSC)[[213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib213)] introduced egocentric segmentation for computing eigenvalues and centroids of segments, employing a GNN to aggregate these features into a descriptor. It outperformed traditional Euclidean clustering in efficiency and robustness for sparse point cloud processing. As shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), Locus [[196](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib196)] encoded topological and temporal information of segments to create a global descriptor using second-order pooling and nonlinear transformation. It avoided global map construction and segment-wise KNN search, achieving robustness to viewpoint changes and occlusions.

Traditional point cloud descriptors relied on low-level properties[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib64), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib106)] to encode the point cloud, but local descriptors lacked description ability, and global descriptors struggled with rotation and translation invariance. Fortunately, segments offered a good compromise between the two. Several observations were summarized as follows:

* • Segments[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74), [195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208), [210](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib210)] offered a potential solution to reduce feature computation by avoiding processing the entire point cloud. Nevertheless, several approaches relied on point cloud aggregation or map construction, leading to inefficiencies when dealing with large-scale environments. * • Segment-based methods showed promise in enhancing accuracy by incorporating geometric, color, and semantic information of segments. However, they required rich 3D geometry structures for segmentation, which might not always be available, thus limiting their applicability. * • Segment-based methods were well-known for their resilience to environmental changes, encompassing illumination, weather, and seasonal variations. However, they offered limited insights into the underlying 3D structures, resulting in subpar segmentation performance during long-term localization scenarios with numerous moving objects.

Segments[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74), [195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208), [210](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib210)] offered a potential solution to reduce feature computation by avoiding processing the entire point cloud. Nevertheless, several approaches relied on point cloud aggregation or map construction, leading to inefficiencies when dealing with large-scale environments.

Segment-based methods showed promise in enhancing accuracy by incorporating geometric, color, and semantic information of segments. However, they required rich 3D geometry structures for segmentation, which might not always be available, thus limiting their applicability.

Segment-based methods were well-known for their resilience to environmental changes, encompassing illumination, weather, and seasonal variations. However, they offered limited insights into the underlying 3D structures, resulting in subpar segmentation performance during long-term localization scenarios with numerous moving objects.

Semantics refers to labels or categories that divide point clouds into various instances using learning-based segmentation technology, facilitating semantic-level place recognition. Thus, semantics-based place recognition falls under the category of learning-based methods. Based on the approach used for semantics association, they can be classified into two types: graph-based and graph-free.
Semantic graphs intuitively depicted the location and topological information of objects. Graph similarity and graph matching were two typical graph operations.

Graph Similarity. X-view[[214](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib214)] computed random walk descriptors for each graph node and determined the similarity score based on the count of identical random walks. It was general in semantic input and mitigated high computational expenses. As depicted in Figure [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.2.2 Classification-based Methods ‣ 5.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), SGPR[[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib53)] represented semantic categories and centroids of points as nodes, capturing node feature relations through edges. It developed a GNN-based graph network with node embedding, graph embedding, and graph-graph interaction to compute graph similarity. SGPR demonstrated robustness against occlusion and viewpoint changes, especially for reverse loops.

Graph Matching. GOSMatch[[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib52)] introduced an object-based place recognition approach for urban environments, which employed graph descriptors for candidate search and vertex descriptors for one-to-one correspondence calculation. BoxGraph[[215](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib215)] stored object shapes in vertices and simplified place recognition to an optimal vertex assignment problem. It employed bounding boxes as appearance embeddings for vertex entities and extended them for pose estimation.
Other works avoided semantic graph construction and mainly fell into two categories: semantic descriptors and other methods.

Semantics Descriptors. As shown in Figure [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.2.2 Classification-based Methods ‣ 5.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), semantic scan context (SSC) [[73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib73), [216](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib216)] enhanced SC [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] by utilizing semantics [[217](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib217)] instead of height. Object scan context (OSC) [[218](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib218)] improved SC [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] by constructing the descriptor around uniformly distributed objects (e.g., street lights and trash cans). It made the descriptor independent of LiDAR’s position and overcame the issue of distant point clouds. Seq-Ndt[[219](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib219)] extended the NDT-based histogram descriptor[[220](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib220)] by incorporating semantic information and utilized the kullback-leibler (KL) divergence to measure similarity. RINet[[221](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib221)] developed a lightweight siamese network with convolution, down-sampling, and attention mechanisms to compute descriptor similarities. It prioritized scene learning over point cloud orientation and was highly efficient, allowing for deployment on resource-constrained platforms.

Other Methods. Recent studies enhanced semantic-based LPR through innovative technologies and theories, including multiple hypothesis trees[[222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib222)], siamese neural network[[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib72), [223](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib223), [224](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib224)], spherical convolution[[225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib225)], and neural tensor network [[226](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib226)].

Inspired by human perception, semantic-based methods utilized pre-defined knowledge databases to categorize objects and identify their topological relationships. However, these methods were still relatively new and immature because they required advanced semantic segmentation technology. Several key observations were summarized below:

* • Graph-based methods[[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib53), [52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib52), [215](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib215)] had streamlined point cloud comprehension but exhibited three limitations: (1) Potential loss of specific features, like object size. (2) Inability to differentiate between parts of the same category leading to information loss. (3) Computing metrics between two graphs remains NP-complete, hindering the precise distance calculation within a reasonable timeframe. * • Semantic labels[[217](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib217)] outperformed using only geometric features, offering more interpretable and intuitive results. They demonstrated greater resilience to occlusion and viewpoint changes, especially in reverse LCD. However, predefined semantic labels in test datasets were limited, failing to encompass various categories in real-life scenarios. * • In dynamic or cluttered environments, leveraging objects and their topological information could enhance recognition accuracy. These methods heavily relied on the outcomes of semantic segmentation, which might lead to poor performance in diverse scenarios. Despite these challenges, they held promise in applications where traditional methods fell short.

Graph-based methods[[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib53), [52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib52), [215](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib215)] had streamlined point cloud comprehension but exhibited three limitations: (1) Potential loss of specific features, like object size. (2) Inability to differentiate between parts of the same category leading to information loss. (3) Computing metrics between two graphs remains NP-complete, hindering the precise distance calculation within a reasonable timeframe.

Semantic labels[[217](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib217)] outperformed using only geometric features, offering more interpretable and intuitive results. They demonstrated greater resilience to occlusion and viewpoint changes, especially in reverse LCD. However, predefined semantic labels in test datasets were limited, failing to encompass various categories in real-life scenarios.

In dynamic or cluttered environments, leveraging objects and their topological information could enhance recognition accuracy. These methods heavily relied on the outcomes of semantic segmentation, which might lead to poor performance in diverse scenarios. Despite these challenges, they held promise in applications where traditional methods fell short.

Trajectory information enables correlating current and recent historical scans for place recognition. Odometry (handcrafted) and sequence (learning) are two prominent usage methods for historical data.

SLAM systems with LCD modules often adopt handcrafted approaches, utilizing front-end poses or traditional registration techniques for place recognition to reduce system complexity. They could be further categorized into naive Euclidean distance, overlap ratio, and PCR-based test.

Comparing the Euclidean distance between real-time and historical poses enabled rough loop closure detection. Some works use piecewise orientation functions[[228](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib228)] and global factor graphs[[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib55)] for pose similarity comparison, while others employ multi-sensor calibration and mapping[[229](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib229)].

The overlap ratio could assess place similarity, with a higher value indicating closer proximity. S4-SLAM[[230](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib230)] implemented a location-based LCD by storing historical poses using a kd tree and evaluating candidate loops based on overlap rate. This approach balanced real-time performance and accuracy, demonstrating robustness even with limited feature points and high moving speeds. Mendes et al.[[231](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib231)] utilized an overlap criterion to generate new keyframes and implemented a graphical model layer over LiDAR odometry to reduce drifts through graph-level loop closing. The hard rejection based on normal angles effectively prevented unexpected drifts arising from vegetation.
PCR techniques verified candidate loops using relative poses, such as standard ICP, point-to-line/plane ICP, and generalized ICP (GICP).

Standard ICP. IN2LAAMA[[232](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib232)] devised an offline probabilistic framework covering localization, mapping, and calibration. It identified loop closures using poses and validated candidates with an optional ICP test ICP[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)], proficiently handling motion distortion without an explicit motion model.

Point-to-Line/Plane ICP. Lego-LOAM [[58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib58)] calculated odometry poses using a two-step Levenberg-Marquardt optimization, comparing historical scans with pose constraints and refining transformations with ICP [[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)]. It was pioneering work to incorporate LCD into LiDAR SLAM, making it well-suited for long-duration navigation tasks. Subsequently, LILO[[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib56)] extended this idea to a LiDAR-IMU system. Other works enhanced registration robustness using plane graphs[[233](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib233)], intuitive weighting[[234](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib234)], and KL divergence[[235](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib235)], respectively.

GICP. As shown in Figure [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S7.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 7 LPR Techniques: Trajectory ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey"), LAMP [[227](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib227)] developed a multi-robot LiDAR SLAM system for challenging subterranean environments that utilized GICP[[236](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib236)] to register nearby scans and proposed an incremental consistent measurement (ICM) set maximization[[237](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib237)] to reject outlying loop closures. Similarly, LAMP 2.0 [[238](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib238)] combined TEASER++ [[239](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib239)] and GICP [[236](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib236)] to compute the relative transform and filter poor matches. SPC-SLAM[[240](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib240)] leveraged the geometric-rigidity-constant assumption[[241](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib241)] and submap registration score[[236](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib236)] to confirm loop closure, addressing high-precision mapping challenges in GNSS-denied environments.

SeqSLAM[[243](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib243)] pioneered visual feature similarity comparisons over time to integrate sequence information and identify the best match within local sequences, showcasing exceptional performance in extreme environmental changes and providing insights for LiDAR-based solutions. The point cloud sequence matching incurred higher computational costs than image-based alternatives. Consequently, approaches such as scan matching and submap matching integrated neural networks with GPUs to enhance efficiency.

As shown in Figure [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S7.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 7.2 Sequence-based Methods ‣ 7 LPR Techniques: Trajectory ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), SeqLPD [[242](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib242)] employed LPD-Net [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5)] for global descriptor extraction and selected super keyframes based on feature space distribution. It combined super keyframe-based coarse matching with the local sequence fine matching to improve detection accuracy and efficiency. This method achieved advanced performance without relying on odometry data. The trained model could be directly applied in real-world scenarios without additional training, facilitating practical applications.

Chen et al.[[244](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib244)] integrated LPD-Net[[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5)] with sequence-based matching and introduced a plane-driven sub-maps matching algorithm to computed relative transformations. This method employed interval stabbing for translation search, demonstrating nearly real-time computation capabilities. As illustrated in Figure [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S7.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 7.2 Sequence-based Methods ‣ 7 LPR Techniques: Trajectory ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), SeqSphereVLAD[[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib6)] and Yin et al.[[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib57)] utilized a spherical convolution module to extract orientation-equivariant local features across multiple layers of spherical perspectives. It effectively handled changing viewpoints and addressed large-scale SLAM challenges. FusionVLAD[[245](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib245)] proposed a multi-view fusion network that encoded top-down and spherical-view features from the local map, enhancing feature combination through a parallel fusion module for end-to-end training. It was well-suited for large-scale mapping tasks with limited computation resources.

Traditional frame-to-frame comparison methods yielded an intuitive similarity score but intended to degrade in closed, symmetric, and dynamic environments. The trajectory-based approaches incorporated both spatial and temporal information to address this limitation. Two observations were summarized as follows:

* • LiDAR SLAM[[227](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib227), [240](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib240)] employed a straightforward LCD method based on pose proximity, followed by PCR for calculating relative transformations. Despite satisfactory results, two limitations remained: (1) Cumulative errors affected the reliability of odometry poses in large-scale scenarios. (2) The local optimality of PCR impeded the integration of loop constraints into global optimization. * • Sequence-based methods exhibited versatility since they effectively incorporated diverse place recognition techniques, such as local and global descriptors[[242](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib242), [57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib57)], semantics, and segments. While visual sequence-based methods had been well-studied, LiDAR-based approaches were still in the early stages. Furthermore, the expensive calculations required for matching and feature fusion restricted their practical applicability.

LiDAR SLAM[[227](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib227), [240](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib240)] employed a straightforward LCD method based on pose proximity, followed by PCR for calculating relative transformations. Despite satisfactory results, two limitations remained: (1) Cumulative errors affected the reliability of odometry poses in large-scale scenarios. (2) The local optimality of PCR impeded the integration of loop constraints into global optimization.

Sequence-based methods exhibited versatility since they effectively incorporated diverse place recognition techniques, such as local and global descriptors[[242](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib242), [57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib57)], semantics, and segments. While visual sequence-based methods had been well-studied, LiDAR-based approaches were still in the early stages. Furthermore, the expensive calculations required for matching and feature fusion restricted their practical applicability.

Map-assisted methods provided global metric localization to achieve place recognition. They generally fall into two groups based on the map construction timing: offline and online maps. Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") illustrates several representative maps.
As the vehicle moved, the static offline map confined its motion within predefined boundaries. Handcrafted methods mainly involved five map types: feature, probability, point cloud, grid, and mesh.

Feature Map. Dong et al.[[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib10)] employed range image-based pole extraction to build a global map and utilized monte carlo localization (MCL) to update particle weights based on pole matching. It demonstrated accurate pole extraction in diverse environments, improving long-term localization performance. Shi et al.[[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib81)] combined RANSAC[[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)] and Euclidean clustering to extract walls from the offline map and online scans, applying point-to-point and point-to-line distance constraints to compute vehicle poses.

Probability Map. As depicted in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), Schmiedel et al.[[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib22)] characterized surface patches in NDT maps using curvature and object shape. They matched descriptors between online scans and the global map, applied RANSAC [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)] for outlier detection, and evaluated matches using a normalized inlier ratio.

Point Cloud Map. Xu et al.[[75](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib75)] introduced a cross-section shape context (CSSC) descriptor that described spatial distribution using elevation and point density, improving recognition performance with two-stage similarity estimation and the nearest cluster distance ratio. As depicted in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), Shi *et al.* [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib82), [249](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib249)] created an offline map database with a kd tree to simulate vehicle orientations and developed a binary loss function to improve localization accuracy.

Grid Map. As shown in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), Aldibaja et al.[[246](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib246)] converted LiDAR scans into image-like representations of road surfaces, incorporating elevation and irradiation data. They employed a shared ID-based XY correlation matrix to represent loop-closure events among map nodes, facilitating large-scale map processing and map-combiner event detection independent of the driving trajectory.

Mesh Map. As depicted in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(d), Chen et al.[[77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib77)] employed Poisson surface reconstruction to generate a mesh map, developing an observation model of an MCL framework. It showcased robust generalization across different LiDAR sensors, eliminating the need for additional training data in varying environments.

SLAM dynamically constructed and updated an online point cloud map of the surrounding environment as the vehicle navigated within unknown terrain. As illustrated in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(e), Multi-metric linear least square (MULLS)[[79](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib79)] incorporated TEASER[[239](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib239)] for loop verification and employed map-to-map ICP[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)] to enhance inter-submap edges with accurate transformations. Continuous-time ICP (CT-ICP) [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib59)] projected a local map onto an elevation image, estimated a 2D transformation using RANSAC [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)], and computed a 6-DoF pose through ICP [[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)] to identify potential loop closures. Liu et al.[[250](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib250)] introduced a real-time 6D SLAM for large-scale natural terrains, which combined rotation histogram matching with a branch and bound search-based ICP[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)] to achieve real-time LCD.
Researchers explored three types of offline maps in learning-based map localization: intensity, point cloud, and node.

Intensity Map. As shown in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(f), Barsan et al.[[247](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib247)] embedded LiDAR intensity maps and online scans into a joint space, using efficient convolutional matching to determine the vehicle’s position. This method achieved centimeter-level accuracy, showcased robustness in handling uncalibrated data, and successfully generalized across various LiDAR sensors.
Point Cloud Map. Three representative methods in this context were monte carlo localization (MCL), kd tree, and pointwise MLP.

*1) MCL*. LocNet[[251](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib251), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib19)] introduced a semi-handcrafted DNN and MCL framework for global localization, utilizing a Gaussian mixture model to represent multiple hypotheses of place recognition. Leveraging learned representations and vehicle poses, it constructed a prior map, achieving high accuracy and efficiency for long-term localization. Sun et al.[[252](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib252)] combined efficient deep deterministic model inference with rigorous geometry verification using a Bayes-filter approach, resolving the non-conjugacy issue between Gaussian and MCL.

*2) Kd Tree*. Jin et al.[[253](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib253)] incorporated the D3feat descriptor[[124](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib124)] with a self-supervised detector loss for feature matching. They employed a kd tree to store map descriptors and improved search efficiency through a coarse-to-fine voting mechanism and a two-phase search strategy.

*3) Pointwise MLP*. L3-Net[[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib26)] utilized a mini-PointNet for feature descriptor extraction and regularized the cost volume with 3D convolutions. It computed matching probabilities for optimal estimation and captured temporal motion dynamics through deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs). L3-Net achieved comparable localization accuracy to SOTA methods and was well-suited for multi-sensor fusion. Retriever[[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib14)] extracted compact features through an encoder and feature propagation network, aggregating them with a perceiver for place recognition in compressed point cloud maps. It improved computing efficiency by avoiding computation-heavy decompression.

Node Map. S4-SLAM2[[254](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib254)] constructed a node map comprising point cloud data, feature vectors, and location information. It extracted geometric and statistical features to create multi-modal descriptors and classified loop closures with a random forest classifier.

OpenStreetMap. OSM, a global open-source map, offered comprehensive geographic details such as streets, railways, water systems, and buildings. Ruchti et al.[[255](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib255)] created a road network and categorized environments as road or non-road, leveraging this classification to weight MCL particles. Several approaches[[256](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib256), [257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib257)] integrated semantic information extracted from OSM into a particle filter framework. As depicted in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(g), Cho et al.[[248](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib248)] generated a descriptor by calculating the distances to buildings at regular angles.
These methods were roughly divided into surfel-based and grid map-based methods.

*1) Surfel Map*. As depicted in Figure [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(h), SuMa[[258](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib258)] and SuMa++[[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib76)] employed range images and surfel-based maps for data association, detecting candidate loops by combining radius search and frame-to-model ICP[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)] registration. They verified loops by tracking poses, which ensured robust detection even with low overlap and yielded globally consistent maps.

*2) Grid Map*. Yin et al.[[259](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib259)] generated a BEV map from the local occupancy map, considering vehicle motion errors. Furthermore, they introduced an additional GAN [[260](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib260)] with conditional entropy reduction to enhance unsupervised feature learning for long-term recognition applications.

Maps[[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib26), [252](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib252), [82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib82)] had been widely used in robot localization and path planning as they offered precise and detailed representations of the environment. Remarkably, map-based methods excelled in recognizing topologically similar localization, providing pose information, and recovering kidnapped robots effectively. Several observations were summarized as follows:

* • Map representations enhanced global consistency and reduced localization errors. However, their large memory requirements resulted in time-consuming loading, communication, and processing. * • Map-based methods cloud overcome noise and partial occlusions, ensuring robust recognition even in challenging scenarios. However, the significant density difference posed difficulties in registering online scans to maps. * • A robust prior map facilitated long-term robot localization in a consistent environment. However, significant environmental changes could cause the existing map to be outdated, resulting in localization and recognition errors.

InCloud[[271](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib271)] distilled the angular relationship between global representations, preserving the complex structure of the embedding space between training steps. It effectively addressed catastrophic forgetting, allowing models to update with new domains without retraining the network on all legacy data. Granström *et al.* [[188](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib188)] encoded the point cloud using geometry features and range histograms, detecting loops with a trained AdaBoost [[189](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib189)] classifier. While achieving high precision and recall rates, this method required the ordered point cloud.
In this section, we summarized existing datasets and evaluation metrics while comparing existing methods on public datasets.

A large number of datasets had been collected to evaluate the performance of LPR methods. Table [III](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S8.T3 "Table III ‣ 8.3 Summary ‣ 8 LPR Techniques: Map ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") provided a summary of these datasets. Their characteristics were summarized as follows:

Long-term Collection. [[263](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib263), [264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib264), [269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib269)] repeatedly gathered the same scenario along similar routes in different seasons or times.

Multi-modal Data. In addition to LiDAR sensors, radar was used in [[267](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib267), [269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib269)] and cameras were mounted in [[261](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib261), [262](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib262), [263](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib263), [264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib264), [268](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib268), [269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib269), [225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib225), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [270](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib270)]. Semantic information was also available in [[266](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib266)].

LiDAR Sparsity.
