In this section, we present several promising trends for future evolution to promote and facilitate further research.
Multi-modality information offers the opportunity to leverage complementary features and enhance the robustness of place recognition and localization. Several novel solutions are as follows:

WiFi. WiFi-based localization retrieves the media access control (MAC) address of routers via the client device (e.g., cellphone) to calculate positions. This solution offers extensive coverage and achieves accurate indoor localization, overcoming GPS signal limitations. Moreover, it is easy to deploy and provides fast localization, holding significant potential for advancing indoor localization industries.

Voice. Voice-based localization uses microphone arrays to capture audio signals, employing delay estimation or spectral analysis to determine sound source locations. It offers advantages like low computational requirements, high concealment, and strong compatibility. Furthermore, it can seamlessly integrate with human-computer interaction systems, smart homes, and other voice-controlled applications, enhancing vehicle situational awareness.

Radio Frequency Identification (RFID). RFID employs radio signals to identify and track objects without physical contact. Its anti-interference capability will ensure reliable autonomous driving in harsh environments. Additionally, the long lifespan can enhance the stability of long-term localization systems. Applying cryptographic encryption to tag data can strengthen system security.
Breaking free from conventional solutions and incorporating interdisciplinary new technologies into autonomous driving holds the potential for unforeseen improvements:

Cloud Computing. Cloud computing offers high-performance shared computing resources to users. Offloading computing tasks to cloud servers enhances robot localization efficiency. With access to powerful computing resources, robots can process diverse high-precision sensor data, thus improving their localization capabilities.

Quantum Technology. Quantum technology revolutionizes information calculation, encoding, and transmission. Quantum sensors can capture subtle changes, delivering ultra-high-precision measurements. Integrating such sensors into robotic navigation will greatly enhance localization and mapping in complex environments.

Bio-inspired Localization. Bio-inspired navigation and group behavior provide novel insights for robot localization. Inspired by turtles’ navigation behavior, robots can enhance localization robustness by employing magnetic field sensors. Multi-robot systems can improve formation stability by emulating the cooperative behavior seen in bird flocks.
Equipping robots with advanced sensors can enhance their navigation capabilities. We present several promising sensors as follows:

Solid-State LiDAR. Unlike mechanical LiDAR, solid-state LiDAR employs a micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS), optical phased array (OPA), or flash technology for signal transmission and reception. It boasts a compact size, high resolution, fast scanning speed, and extended measurement range. It enables precise identification of buildings, pedestrians, vehicles, and traffic signs, effectively ensuring autonomous driving safety, supporting smart transportation data, and monitoring traffic accidents.

Event Camera. Instead of conventional fixed-frequency acquisition, event cameras exclusively generate an asynchronous event stream when notable visual changes occur. They offer numerous benefits, including high time resolution, low latency, wide dynamic range, and low power consumption. Equipping vehicles with event cameras enhances obstacle avoidance in high-speed scenarios, enables navigation through scenes with abrupt light changes, and facilitates handling emergencies.

Millimeter Wave Radar. Millimeter-wave radar employs frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) signals and mixers to measure speed, distance, and direction, providing cost-effectiveness, precise longitudinal ranging, accurate object detection, weather resistance, and high bandwidth. It will find wide applications in blind spot detection, object detection and tracking, parking assistance, and adaptive cruise control.
As a new scientific and technological revolution unfolds, robot technology will spearhead advancements in several critical fields shaping the fate of humanity:

Space Exploration. In inhospitable environments like the moon, robots will assume the role of humans, undertaking tasks such as terrain mapping, mineral identification, house construction, and 3D printing. They will aid human understanding of deep space and other planets.

Polar Research. Robots advance polar research by enhancing data collection capabilities. They collect data on glaciers, weather, and temperature, facilitating continuous environmental monitoring. High-resolution mapping of polar topography helps identify landform changes, glacier movement, and geological processes.

Underwater Robots. Underwater robots are advanced submersibles tailored for extreme underwater operations. The fiber optic gyroscope and Doppler log will greatly enhance localization performance, benefiting port construction and naval defense. Sonar detection technology will further improve task efficiency like underwater rescue and pipeline maintenance.
A fair and thorough evaluation is crucial for adapting robot products, algorithms, and scenarios. Here are three pivotal considerations for future algorithm evaluation.

Scalability and Efficiency. The growing affordability and accessibility of LiDAR sensors have spurred the demand for large-scale place recognition. This necessitates the development of scalable algorithms for handling large-scale point clouds and the design of efficient algorithms for the real-time processing of point cloud data on resource-constrained platforms.

Long-term Place Recognition. Long-term place recognition refers to the ability of a system to identify places over extended periods, despite appearance and weather variations. It is a crucial capability for autonomous navigation. Designing algorithms that can handle seasons, weather, appearances, and dynamic objects, will drive significant advancements in this field.

Standardized Datasets. A good dataset should possess sufficient size, high-quality data, reliable ground truth, annotations or labels, ethical considerations, normalized form, and clear instructions. Creating diverse data encompassing various sensor modalities, environmental conditions, and weather changes is also highly valuable.
Learning-based LPR methods have demonstrated impressive results, and we outline promising directions to improve their performance as follows:

Network Design. Transformer-based networks [[166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [155](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib155), [165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169)] are computationally expensive for large-scale datasets. To address this, techniques like model compression and efficient attention mechanisms can be used to reduce computational requirements.

Loss Function. The lazy quadruplet loss[[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13), [172](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib172), [165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166)] is prone to overfitting with limited training data. Regularization techniques like weight decay, dropout, or batch normalization may enhance generalization performance.

Training Strategy. End-to-end networks[[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68), [151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151), [162](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib162), [152](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib152), [168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168), [174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174)] commonly demand large amounts of labeled data for training. Transfer learning and semi-supervised learning may enhance training efficiency.

This paper is the first comprehensive survey specifically dedicated to LPR research to the best of our knowledge. It provides extensive discussions on the background of place recognition, highlighting the primary concerns in current research. We conduct a comprehensive method classification and performance comparison, elucidating their architectures, strengths, and weaknesses. Furthermore, we summarize commonly employed datasets, evaluation metrics, and promising future directions.

chunks.text: # LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

LiDAR-based place recognition (LPR) plays a pivotal role in autonomous driving, which assists Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems in reducing accumulated errors and achieving reliable localization. However, existing reviews predominantly concentrate on visual place recognition (VPR) methods. Despite the recent remarkable progress in LPR, to the best of our knowledge, there is no dedicated systematic review in this area. This paper bridges the gap by providing a comprehensive review of place recognition methods employing LiDAR sensors, thus facilitating and encouraging further research. We commence by delving into the problem formulation of place recognition, exploring existing challenges, and describing relations to previous surveys. Subsequently, we conduct an in-depth review of related research, which offers detailed classifications, strengths and weaknesses, and architectures. Finally, we summarize existing datasets, commonly used evaluation metrics, and comprehensive evaluation results from various methods on public datasets. This paper can serve as a valuable tutorial for newcomers entering the field of place recognition and for researchers interested in long-term robot localization. We pledge to maintain an up-to-date project on our website https://github.com/ShiPC-AI/LPR-Survey.

## 1 Introduction

Place recognition [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib1), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib2), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib3), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib6), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7), [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib8)] is a challenging and ongoing research problem that aims to identify previously visited places across different viewpoints and environments. This task holds great significance in various robotic applications. Firstly, long-term localization [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib10), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib11)] and place retrieval [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13), [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib14)] address the issue of localization in changing environments. Secondly, place recognition[[15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib15), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib16), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib17), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18)] facilitates real-time loop closure detection (LCD) to create drift-free global maps. Thirdly, metric localization [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib19), [20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib20), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib21)] within prior maps offers a reliable means to recover the kidnapped vehicle’s poses.

Sensor observation-based methods [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib22), [23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib23), [24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib24), [25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib25), [26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib26), [27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib27)] outperform traditional global positioning system (GPS)[[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib28), [29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib29), [30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib30)], inertia measurement unit (IMU)[[31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib31), [32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib32), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib33), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib34)], and wheel odometers[[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib35)] in autonomy, flexibility, anti-interference capability, independence from geomagnetic signals, and cost-effectiveness. Despite significant research advancements and the emergence of numerous methods in recent years, place recognition remains challenging due to viewpoint differences, occlusions, data variations, long-term changes, and computational complexity. To facilitate and encourage further research, scholars have engaged in method classification[[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib36)], performance evaluation[[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib37), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib38)], challenge summarization[[39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib39)], and prospect prediction [[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib40)] based on the current progress in this field. However, existing work primarily focuses on visual place recognition (VPR), necessitating a comprehensive and systematic review of LiDAR-based place recognition (LPR) to bridge this gap.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of LPR research, accompanied by a detailed methodological taxonomy depicted in Figure [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey"). We categorize methods into handcrafted and learning-based types, further subdividing them, and present detailed introductions to pioneering works. This well-organized layout enhances reading efficiency and facilitates a better understanding of the relevant technologies in place recognition. Our main contributions are as follows:

* • To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first survey exclusively focusing on place recognition based on 3D LiDAR. We delve into the problem formulation, challenges, and the relationship to previous surveys. * • We provide an in-depth overview of LPR covering conventional handcrafted descriptors and advanced deep-learning techniques. We classify existing methods into seven categories and describe their advantages and limitations. * • We incorporate numerous figures and tables to help readers understand the open-source code, backbone networks, feature types, similarity metrics, memory costs, training strategies, running efficiency, and localization capabilities of these methods. * • We summarize existing datasets and evaluation metrics while comprehensively comparing existing methods on several public datasets. In addition, we also provide a regularly updated project.

To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first survey exclusively focusing on place recognition based on 3D LiDAR. We delve into the problem formulation, challenges, and the relationship to previous surveys.

We provide an in-depth overview of LPR covering conventional handcrafted descriptors and advanced deep-learning techniques. We classify existing methods into seven categories and describe their advantages and limitations.

We incorporate numerous figures and tables to help readers understand the open-source code, backbone networks, feature types, similarity metrics, memory costs, training strategies, running efficiency, and localization capabilities of these methods.

We summarize existing datasets and evaluation metrics while comprehensively comparing existing methods on several public datasets. In addition, we also provide a regularly updated project.

The structure of this paper is as follows. Section [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") summarizes our contributions and paper structures. Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S2 "2 Background ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") describes the research background. From Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S3 "3 LPR Techniques: Local Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") to [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S9 "9 LPR Techniques: Other Methods ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey"), we comprehensively review recent methods and offer detailed classifications. Section [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S10 "10 Benchmarking ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") collects existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance comparisons on public datasets. Finally, Section [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S11 "11 Future Directions ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") presents promising future directions and Section [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S12 "12 Conclusions ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") concludes the paper.

chunks.text:
### 2.2 Challenges of LPR

With the advancements in image processing technologies[[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib41)] and the availability of affordable equipment, numerous vision-based methods[[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib42), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib1), [43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib43), [44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib44)] have emerged over the past decades. However, they encounter challenges such as illumination variations, viewpoint changes, adverse weather conditions, and scale ambiguity. In contrast, LiDAR sensors actively emit laser signals to capture high-resolution 3D points, which excel in providing precise and detailed geometric information [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib45)] even in low-light conditions. In addition, the rapid progress of 3D scanning technology further fuels the interest in place recognition research using LiDAR sensors.

Numerous recent LPR methods have explored techniques like bird-eye-view (BEV) [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib47)], histograms[[48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib49)], image representations[[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)], and graph theory [[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51), [52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib52), [53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib53)] to enhance performance. They achieve rotational invariance through brute-force search[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46)] and frequency domain analysis[[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib47), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib54)]. Additional approaches employ pose proximity[[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib55), [56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib56)], sequence matching[[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib6), [57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib57)], and point cloud registration (PCR)[[58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib58), [59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib59), [60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib60)] techniques to improve recognition accuracy. However, these methods struggle in dynamic and highly occluded environments. Traditional methods rely on low-level features (coordinates[[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib61)], normals[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62)], intensities[[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib63), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib64), [65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65)], range[[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib66)] and density[[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib67)]), while learning-based approaches gradually show promising results using neural networks[[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib69)], attention mechanisms[[70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70), [71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71)], semantics[[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib72), [73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib73)], and classifiers[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)]. Furthermore, diverse map representations, such as point clouds[[75](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib75)], semantics[[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib76)], and mesh[[77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib77)], have been successfully applied in map localization. Despite the impressive results claimed by these methods, several challenges persist that require further attention:

* • Motion Distortions: The common assumption of constant velocity motion [[78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib78), [79](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib79)] is inaccurate for deskewing distorted scans, especially in high-speed applications. * • Viewpoint Differences: Lane-level horizontal deviations may exist when a robot revisits a historical place from different directions. While a few methods [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51)] address rotation invariance, they overlook the impact of translation on place recognition. * • Weather Conditions: Laser signals exhibit varying behavior under different weather conditions[[80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib80)]. They attenuate less and travel farther on sunny days but decay significantly in rainy and foggy weather. * • Perceptual Aliasing: Distinct places in confined corridors[[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib81), [82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib82)] may exhibit similar point cloud data, which introduces ambiguous interpretations. * • Appearance Changes: Long-term navigation applications[[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib10), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib38), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib11)] often involve significant environmental changes, which leads to potential failures. * • Sensor Characteristics. Mechanical LiDAR[[83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib83), [58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib58)] produces point clouds in a format of multiple scan lines, resulting in vertical sparsity. Solid-state LiDAR[[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84)] provides limited horizontal field-of-view (FOV) and requires specific considerations in the recognition process.

Motion Distortions: The common assumption of constant velocity motion [[78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib78), [79](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib79)] is inaccurate for deskewing distorted scans, especially in high-speed applications.

Viewpoint Differences: Lane-level horizontal deviations may exist when a robot revisits a historical place from different directions. While a few methods [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib51)] address rotation invariance, they overlook the impact of translation on place recognition.

Weather Conditions: Laser signals exhibit varying behavior under different weather conditions[[80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib80)]. They attenuate less and travel farther on sunny days but decay significantly in rainy and foggy weather.

Perceptual Aliasing: Distinct places in confined corridors[[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib81), [82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib82)] may exhibit similar point cloud data, which introduces ambiguous interpretations.

Appearance Changes: Long-term navigation applications[[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib10), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib38), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib11)] often involve significant environmental changes, which leads to potential failures.

Sensor Characteristics. Mechanical LiDAR[[83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib83), [58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib58)] produces point clouds in a format of multiple scan lines, resulting in vertical sparsity. Solid-state LiDAR[[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84)] provides limited horizontal field-of-view (FOV) and requires specific considerations in the recognition process.

### 2.3 Relation to Previous Surveys

In recent years, there has been a proliferation of reviews on visual robotics technologies, addressing various topics such as place recognition[[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib37), [40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib40), [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib36), [39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib39)], localization[[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib85), [86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib86)], tracking[[87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib87), [88](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib88)], and SLAM [[89](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib89), [90](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib90), [91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib91)]. While these reviews have made significant contributions to the progress of research in robotics and autonomous driving, they have regrettably neglected the technology of LiDAR sensors.

Cadena *et al.*[[92](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib92)] extensively reviewed the current state of SLAM and delved into potential future directions. Yin et al.[[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib93)] provided a comprehensive place recognition survey encompassing cameras, LiDAR, radar, and joint sensors. However, the section dedicated to discussing LiDAR was relatively limited. Yin et al.[[94](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib94)] offered an informative overview of the recent progress and advancements in LiDAR-based global localization, while it merely represented a specialized branch of place recognition. Distinct from previous works, our survey solely focused on LiDAR-based place recognition research. It provided a comprehensive overview of the problem formulation, task challenges, method classifications, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, experimental performances, and future directions.

chunks.text:
## 3 LPR Techniques: Local Descriptor

The local descriptor is a compact representation of regions or points, capturing distinctive characteristics such as texture, color, density, or shape. Local descriptor-based methods typically extract keypoints and employ local descriptors to characterize their surrounding context. They generally fell into either 3D-based or 2D-based categories based on the nature of descriptors. Table [I](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S2.T1 "Table I ‣ 2.3 Relation to Previous Surveys ‣ 2 Background ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") contained a systematic summary. Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Relation to Previous Surveys ‣ 2 Background ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey") described several representative methods.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text: ### 3.1 Handcrafted Methods

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 3.1.1 3D-based Methods

We roughly categorize handcrafted 3D local descriptors into two groups based on a local reference frame (LRF).

LRF-based Methods. LRF aimed to rigidly transform the patch into its canonical representation by selecting neighborhood points to build a covariance matrix and computing the eigenvector as reference axes. While initially designed for PCR, it was also applicable to place recognition. Several methods focused on encoding geometric information, such as normal[[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib103), [63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib63)], height[[105](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib105)], and mesh[[102](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib102)], within the LRF to achieve precise geometric descriptions. Others enhanced the stability of LRF using weighted projection vectors[[104](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib104)] or sign disambiguation[[101](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib101)].

LRF-free Methods. Other methods ensured rotation invariance by avoiding LRF construction and focusing solely on the underlying geometry of the local surface. Early methods directly counted surrounding geometric information, such as height[[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib61)], distance[[97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib97), [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib98), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib3)], and density[[95](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib95)], as local surface descriptions. Subsequently, several methods encoded point distribution[[96](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib96), [100](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib100)] and sparse triangulated landmark[[99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib99)].

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 3.1.2 2D-based Methods

These methods projected a point cloud to a 2D image and built handcrafted local descriptors from the image, followed by an image matching problem. Spherical view and bird-eye-view (BEV) were two representative projection approaches.

Spherical View. Projecting point clouds into a spherical or range image using a bearing angle (BA) model effectively mitigated orientation ambiguity. Steder et al.[[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib106)] pioneered the projection of point clouds to range images for place recognition. They extracted the local descriptor vector [[132](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib132)] and evaluated candidate transformations through keypoint reprojection. Afterward, several works extended the method[[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib106)] using normal aligned radial features (NARF) [[15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib15)], speeded up robust features (SURF) [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib107)] and ORB[[108](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib108), [109](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib109)].

BEV. Several works incorporated proposal-wise features from BEV images into image matching. BVMatch[[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib54)] extracted the maximum index map[[133](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib133)] of the Log-Gabor filter responses, employing BEV feature transform and BoW for place recognition. This approach provided relative poses and effectively overcame sparsity and intensity distortion. Luo et al.[[49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib49)] applied features from accelerated segment test (FAST)[[134](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib134)] detectors on the BEV image and constructed a HOPN descriptor using 3D normals. It showcased superior localization capability in large-scale scenarios.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text: ### 3.2 Learning-based Methods

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 3.2.1 3D-based Methods

Learning-based 3D local descriptors typically employ 3D CNNs to encode point cloud patches, divided into voxel grids and raw 3D points according to network inputs.

Voxel Grids. The pioneering work 3DMatch[[112](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib112)] transformed patches into voxel grids of truncated signed distance function (TSDF) and employed eight convolutional layers to learn local descriptors. Subsequently, several works extended this idea to more informative encoding manner such as binary occupancy[[111](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib111)], multi-label occupancy [[110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib110)], sparse tensor representation[[113](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib113)], smoothed density value[[114](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib114)], and spherical voxelization[[115](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib115), [116](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib116)].

Raw 3D Points. An alternative method involved direct processing of the raw point cloud data.

*1) PointNet Family*. PointNet[[117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib117)] was a pioneering work of learning from unordered point clouds, which learned a symmetry function approximated by a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to handle detailed shapes. Subsequently, PointNet++ [[118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib118)] introduced an enhanced version that used ball query search to apply PointNet[[117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib117)] recursively and aggregated features from multiple scales. Several works extended PointNet[[117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib117)] by normals[[120](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib120)], FoldingNet decoder[[121](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib121)], orientation[[123](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib123)], LRF[[125](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib125), [126](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib126)], and semantics[[122](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib122)].

*2) Other Methods*. Compact Geometric Features (CGF)[[119](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib119)] trained a deep network to map from the high-dimensional space of spherical histograms to a low-dimensional Euclidean space. D3Feat[[124](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib124)] designed a dual-role fully convolutional network that densely predicted both detection scores and description features. Local equivariant descriptor (LEAD)[[127](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib127)] combined spherical CNNs to learn the equivariant representation and utilized plane-folding decoders for unsupervised learning.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 3.2.2 2D-based Methods

Several works inferred local descriptors using well-established 2D CNNs from projected 2D images. They demonstrated superior performance in the task of 3D shape recognition and retrieval. LORAX[[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib25)] and DeLightLCD[[131](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib131)] employed a deep neural network (DNN) auto-encoder and attention to enhance descriptor descriptiveness on 2D depth images, respectively. Another spectrum of research fused multi-view features into local descriptors by soft-view pooling[[129](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib129)], graphical model[[128](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib128)], and spectral relaxation[[130](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib130)].

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
### 3.3 Summary

This section reviewed some representative methods and more comprehensive surveys of local descriptors were available in [[135](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib135), [136](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib136), [137](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib137)]. Although local descriptors found wide applications in tasks such as PCR and object recognition, they were not the preferred methods for place recognition. There were mainly the following reasons:

* • Viewpoint changes could affect the accuracy of 3D keypoints[[138](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib138)], rendering them unsuitable for matching. Moreover, they might not effectively handle data noise and object occlusions. * • The usage of 3D local descriptors[[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib61), [99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib99)] could be challenging as it required dense point clouds, which was computationally expensive and might not work well with sensors like Velodyne VLP-16[[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib66)] that produced sparse point clouds. * • While converting point clouds into images [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib106), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib54), [131](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib131)] could use mature image processing techniques, this resulted in the loss of geometric information, making it unsuitable for large-scale scenarios.

### 4.1 Handcrafted Methods

Handcrafted global descriptors usually used a single descriptor to describe the entire point cloud. According to the type of space division, they could be divided into BEV-based, discretization-based, and point-based methods. Three representative methods were shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods

BEV projection gained significant attention in the robotics community due to its ability to enhance algorithm efficiency through dimension reduction, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Scan Context (SC)[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] family and pairwise matching were two mainstream methods.

SC Family. As illustrated in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), the pioneering work SC[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] partitioned the horizontal space into discrete bins while maintaining the points’ maximum height to generate a 2D matrix descriptor. It utilized the ring key to search for potential matches and conducted a column-wise comparison to identify the closest one. This method demonstrated promising performance but might fail when dealing with significant lateral offsets. Subsequently, researchers proposed a series of SC-based variant methods, which employed the polar and cart context[[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7)], intensities[[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)], frequency domain[[144](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib144)], local reference frame (LRF)[[139](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib139)], F-norm [[143](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib143)], and spatial binary pattern (SBP) [[145](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib145)] to enhance performance. Furthermore, certain studies [[175](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib175), [176](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib176), [177](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib177)] had incorporated SC-based methods into the LCD module of LiDAR SLAM frameworks to enhance the performance of localization and map construction.

Pairwise Matching. LiDAR Iris[[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib47)] drew inspiration from human iris signatures, utilizing LoG-Gabor filtering and thresholding to create binary signature images, then measuring descriptor similarities using Hamming distance. Some methods also employed weighted distances[[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib67)] and orientation-invariant metrics[[141](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib141), [142](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib142)] for pairwise similarity computation.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.1.2 Discretization-based Methods

The discretization processing transformed the point cloud into 3D discrete representations, categorized into fixed and unfixed size-based approaches.

Fixed-size Discretization. Magnussonet al.[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146)] mapped the point cloud to normal distribution transform (NDT) voxels and created a histogram based on the probability density function of the local surface. They calculated the descriptor similarities using weighted Euclidean distances. This method demonstrated the potential of NDT descriptors for place recognition. Subsequently, researchers introduced techniques like k-means++ clustering[[178](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib178)] and normalized cross-correlation metrics[[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [179](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib179)] to enhance generalization. Cao et al.[[148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] also generated a numerical descriptor by detecting contours and computing spectrum energies from wedge-shaped voxels.

Unfixed-size Discretization. As depicted in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.1 BEV-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), DELIGHT [[64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib64), [147](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib147)] divided the support region into two concentric spheres and got non-overlapping bins by horizontal and azimuthal divisions. It computed intensity histograms for each bin and assessed descriptor similarities by chi-squared tests. Notably, the descriptor could be local or global based on the descriptor’s radius and center point.

chunks.text:
### 4.2 Learning-based Methods

This section explored learning-based methods for obtaining global descriptors, categorized into five groups based on network architecture and model mechanism: point-based, discretization-based, classification-based, projection-based, and fusion-based methods.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.2.1 Point-based Methods

One prevalent approach directly utilized the inherent 3D spatial information for LiDAR point cloud processing, involving point-wise MLP, point convolution, and graph representation, as shown in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").

Pointwise MLP. The pioneering end-to-end work PointNetVLAD [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12)] combined PointNet [[117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib117)] for local feature extraction and NetVLAD[[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib43)] for global descriptor generation. It employed metric learning [[180](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib180)] and introduced the lazy triplet and quadruplet loss functions to enhance the generality of global descriptors. Afterward, PCAN[[70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70)] and SOE-Net[[151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151)] improved high-dimensional feature representation by incorporating attention mechanisms. As depicted in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), LCD-Net[[152](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib152)] utilized the PointVoxel-RCNN (PV-RCNN)[[181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib181)] architecture and combined the feature extraction capabilities of deep neural network with transport theory algorithms.

Point Convolution. DH3D[[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71)] introduced a Siamese network for local feature detection, description, and global descriptor extraction in a single forward pass. It incorporated multi-level spatial contextual information and channel-wise feature correlations using flex convolution (FlexConv)[[182](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib182)] and squeeze-and-excitation (SE)[[183](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib183)]. As shown in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), EPC-Net[[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib69)] was a compact model based on edge convolution, simplifying the process with spatial-adjacent matrices and proxy points. It achieved excellent performance while significantly reducing computational memory.

Graph Representation. Graph networks efficiently capture underlying geometric and shape properties, allowing for effective processing and feature comparison across multiple locations within graphs. As illustrated in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.3 Point-based Methods ‣ 4.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), LPD-Net[[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5)] and vLPD-Net[[154](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib154)] combined adaptive local feature extraction with a graph-based neighborhood aggregation module. They extracted multiple local features, including curvature, height, and density, and employed a graph neural network (GNN) for feature aggregation. Several works integrated an attention module to discern task-relevant features[[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13)], learn spatial relationships between regions[[155](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib155)], and mitigate the influence of movable noises[[153](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib153)].

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.2.2 Discretization-based Methods

We divided discretization-based methods into sparse and dense representations based on voxel density.

Sparse Representation. Three approaches for generating global descriptors using 3D CNNs on sparse volume representations were feature pyramid network (FPN), transformer network, and other methods.

*1) FPN*. MinkLoc3D[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156)], a pioneering work based on sparse voxelization, employed a 3D FPN[[184](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib184)] architecture and generalized-mean (GeM)[[185](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib185)] pooling for global descriptor generation. It showcased a simple and elegant architecture, highlighting the potential of sparse voxelized representation and sparse convolutions for efficient 3D feature extraction. Later works extended MinkLoc3D[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156)] by incorporating intensity[[161](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib161)], image[[157](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib157)], and attention[[158](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib158), [160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib160)] to enhance recognition performance.

*2) Transformer Network*. TransLoc3D[[159](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib159)] re-weighted features from multiple receptive scales using an attention map and incorporated external attention layers for capturing long-range contextual information. SVT-Net[[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib8)], illustrated in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.2 Discretization-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), introduced two types of transformers to capture short-range local features and long-range contextual features, respectively. Despite a shallow network architecture, it generated descriptive descriptors.

*3) Other Methods*. LoGG3D-Net[[162](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib162)] utilized sparse U-Net[[186](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib186)] for high-dimensional feature embedding and introduced a local consistency loss for feature similarity maximization. It exhibited superior end-to-end performance, operating in near real-time.

Dense Representation. Likewise, we broadly categorized dense representation-based approaches into transformer network, DNN, and other methods.

*1) Transformer Network*. HiTPR [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165)] utilized a short-range transformer to extract local features within cells and a long-range transformer to encode global relations among the cells. It enhanced the relevance of local neighbors and global contextual dependencies, showcasing its superior effectiveness. As shown in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.2 Discretization-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), NDT-Transformer[[166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166)] introduced a novel network with three stacked transformer encoders, learning a global descriptor from discrete NDT cells. It struck a valuable balance between state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance and runtime, making it a valuable addition to NDT-based SLAM and MCL methods.

*2) DNN*. SpoxelNet[[163](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib163)] voxelized the point cloud in spherical coordinates, representing voxel occupancy using ternary values. It extracted multi-scale structural features and generated a global descriptor by concatenating features from various directions. This method effectively handled occlusion and moving objects in crowded indoor spaces.

*3) Other Methods*. Voxel-based representation learning (VBRL)[[164](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib164)] tackled long-term place recognition by jointly learning voxel importance and feature modalities using structured sparsity-inducing norms. It integrated all features into a unified regularized optimization formulation.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.2.3 Classification-based Methods

Several approaches addressed the place recognition problem using classifiers. FastLCD [[65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65)] encoded multi-modality features into a global descriptor, detecting candidate loop closures using supervised learning and rejecting false positives through cross-validation and post-verification. On the other hand, Habich et al.[[187](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib187)] used a compact global descriptor[[188](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib188)] to encode each LiDAR scan, performed loop searches within a variable radius based on the largest eigenvalue of the position covariance matrix and predicted loop events using an AdaBoost[[189](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib189)] classifier.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.2.4 Projection-based Methods

Following the taxonomy of learning-based 2D local descriptors (Section [3.1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S3.SS1.SSS2 "3.1.2 2D-based Methods ‣ 3.1 Handcrafted Methods ‣ 3 LPR Techniques: Local Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")), this section also categorized projection methods into spherical view and BEV.

Spherical View. Using spherical projection images as input, three representative methods included siamese network, transformer network, and 2D CNN only.

*1) Siamese Network*. Yin et al.[[167](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib167)] transformed the point cloud into a one-channel image using range distribution and spherical coordinates. They used a Siamese CNN to convert LCD into a similarity modeling problem, improving search efficiency by combining Euclidean metric and kd-tree. MMCS-Net[[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168)] incorporated a Siamese CNN with shallow-deep feature fusion and a cascaded attention mechanism to handle pseudo images. It effectively encoded targeted features for challenging scenes, striking a favorable balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

*2) Transformer Network*. SeqOT[[169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169)] employed multi-scale transformers to generate sub-descriptors that fuse spatial and temporal information from sequential LiDAR range images. The yaw-rotation-invariant architecture ensured robustness to viewpoint changes and scan order, enabling reliable place recognition even in opposite directions. As depicted in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2.4 Projection-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), OverlapTransformer[[170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170)] applied a modified OverlapNetLeg to extract features from range images and integrated a transformer module to capture relative feature locations and global information. It demonstrated fast running speed and robust generalization across diverse environments. Attention-based deep learning network (AttDLNet)[[171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] also incorporated a four-layer attention network to capture long-range context and inter-feature relationships.

*3) 2D CNN Only*. OREOS[[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50)] used 2D convolutional and max pooling layers to extract features from 2D range images, enhancing the descriptor performance via a triple loss function and strong negative mining strategy. It efficiently computed the descriptor while enabling long-term 3-DoF metric localization in outdoor environments.

BEV. Two representative BEV-based methods were encoder-decoder network and 2D CNN only.

*1) Encoder-Decoder Network*. As shown in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2.4 Projection-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), differentiable scan context with orientation (DiSCO)[[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68)] employed an encoder-decoder network to extract descriptors and estimated relative orientation through Fourier-Mellin Transform and differentiable phase correlation. It enhanced the interpretability and efficiency of the feature extractor.

*2) 2D CNN Only*. Scan context image (SCI)[[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)] extended SC[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)] into three channels, enabling robot localization on a grid map through a convolutional neural network-based place classification. It demonstrated robust year-round localization with only a single day of learning.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 4.2.5 Fusion-based Methods

These methods combined LiDAR and image features to enhance descriptor capabilities. Several works transformed the point cloud into an image and only utilized a 2D network for descriptor extraction. CORAL[[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18)] used ResNet18[[190](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib190)] to extract multi-scale features from elevation and visual images. Bernreiteret al.[[173](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib173)] employed spherical CNNs[[191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib191), [192](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib192), [193](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib193)] to learn a multi-modal descriptor from spherical and visual images. As depicted in Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.2.5 Fusion-based Methods ‣ 4.2 Learning-based Methods ‣ 4 LPR Techniques: Global Descriptor ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey"), another line of research involved employing both 2D and 3D networks. Adafusion[[174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174)] and PIC-Net[[172](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib172)] incorporated an attention mechanism to learn adaptive feature weights and created a compound descriptor using two types of networks.

chunks.text:
### 4.3 Summary

Global descriptors were currently the most popular place recognition method, which could provide information about the entire scene, unaffected by local changes. The progress of deep learning in 3D computer vision paved the way for data-driven methods in LPR. Several observations were summarized as follows:

For the handcrafted part:

* • BEV[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)] demonstrated superior performance in flat structural environments but has three main limitations: (1) When the z-axis of the LiDAR changed in the global coordinate system, poor results might arise because these methods assumed local planar vehicle motion. (2) Large lateral offsets might cause missed loops or failed re-localization. (3) Rotation matching could only compute yaw angles, leading to potential local optimum issues if used as initial poses for iterative closest point (ICP)[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)]. * • Discretization-based methods[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146), [84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] could describe the local surface using robust mathematical theories. However, increasing the resolution would significantly incur a heavy computational burden. * • Point-based methods[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] were the most basic global descriptor methods. However, they required expensive neighbor searching to establish topological relationships. Furthermore, projection operations [[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] might result in information loss and cause potential false positives.

BEV[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib7), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib46), [140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib140)] demonstrated superior performance in flat structural environments but has three main limitations: (1) When the z-axis of the LiDAR changed in the global coordinate system, poor results might arise because these methods assumed local planar vehicle motion. (2) Large lateral offsets might cause missed loops or failed re-localization. (3) Rotation matching could only compute yaw angles, leading to potential local optimum issues if used as initial poses for iterative closest point (ICP)[[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib194)].

Discretization-based methods[[146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib146), [84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib84), [148](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib148)] could describe the local surface using robust mathematical theories. However, increasing the resolution would significantly incur a heavy computational burden.

Point-based methods[[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib62), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib48), [149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] were the most basic global descriptor methods. However, they required expensive neighbor searching to establish topological relationships. Furthermore, projection operations [[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib149), [150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib150)] might result in information loss and cause potential false positives.

For the learning part:

* • Learning-based methods delivered impressive efficiency and accurate recognition but heavily relied on ample training samples and extensive data cleaning. Real-world environments presented additional challenges, including noise, occlusions, and uncertainties in LiDAR measurements. Consequently, transfer learning might be necessary for specific applications. * • Transformers [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166), [169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] excelled at capturing long-range dependencies and contextual relationships, enabling reliable recognition in cluttered environments. However, their substantial computational demands constrained the batch size for metric learning. * • Sparse convolutional architectures[[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib156), [161](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib161), [157](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib157), [160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib160)] excelled at generating informative local features while struggling to discriminate feature size in dynamic scenarios. Additionally, simply stacking convolution layers might neglect long-range contextual information. * • Point-based methods [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib12), [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib70), [151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib151), [71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib71), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib5), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib13)] were permutation invariant and could handle unordered point clouds but lacked explicit capture of local spatial relationships. Classification-based methods [[65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib65), [187](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib187)] assigned higher weights to informative features during training, emphasizing discriminative features. However, the specific contribution of each weak classifier to the overall prediction might be less interpretable. * • Projection-based methods[[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib168), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib50), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib68), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib9)] had lower computational complexity and offered more interpretable results. However, they might suffer from information loss due to dimensionality reduction. Fusion-based methods[[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib18), [174](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib174), [173](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib173)] harnessed the complementary strengths of different sensors. Nevertheless, achieving consistent data association in dynamic environments remained challenging.

Real-world environments presented additional challenges, including noise, occlusions, and uncertainties in LiDAR measurements. Consequently, transfer learning might be necessary for specific applications.

Transformers [[165](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib165), [166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib166), [169](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib169), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib170), [171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib171)] excelled at capturing long-range dependencies and contextual relationships, enabling reliable recognition in cluttered environments. chunks.text:
## 5 LPR Techniques: Segments

Segments are meaningful region divisions characterized by similar geometric properties. These methods divide the point cloud into segments and three representative methods are shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey").

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
### 5.1 Handcrafted Methods

These approaches generally extracted segment features for place recognition and could be divided into matching-based and similarity-based methods.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 5.1.1 Matching-based Methods

Segment-based matching for finding correspondences primarily comprised the SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] family and other methods.

SegMatch Family. The pioneering work SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)], depicted in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(a), employed Euclidean clustering to partition the point cloud into segments and extracted eigenvalue-based features. It effectively identified potential correspondences using random forest and random sample consensus (RANSAC)[[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)]-based geometric verification. Dubé et al.[[198](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib198)] enhanced SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] by tracking a single segment using region-growing-based incremental segmentation. Moreover, certain studies effectively integrated SegMatch[[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib74)] into traditional LiDAR SLAM[[199](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib199)] and multi-robot systems [[200](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib200)].

Other Methods. DL-SLAM [[201](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib201)] employed k-means to extract segments from a 2.5D heightmap and defined five descriptors to facilitate segment matching. RDC-SLAM[[202](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib202)] combined an eigenvalue-based segment descriptor, k nearest neighbors (KNN) search, and RANSAC-based verification[[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib197)] to refine relative poses. It accurately fused information from multiple robots without prior knowledge. Gong et al.[[203](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib203)] constructed a spatial relation graph to represent segments, effectively capturing general spatial relations between irregular clusters.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 5.1.2 Similarity-based Methods

Seed [[204](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib204)] developed a segmentation-based egocentric descriptor, incorporating topological information into SC-based place recognition[[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib4)]. It achieved translation and rotation invariance by utilizing the inner topological structure of segmented objects.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
### 5.2 Learning-based Methods

Neural network application on segments primarily involved matching, classification, and similarity computation.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 5.2.1 Matching-based Methods

Tinchev et al.[[205](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib205)] encoded geometric properties and point distribution of segments to extract repeatable oriented key poses, which were matched using reliable shape descriptors and a Random Forest. However, significant changes in the sensor’s vantage point could negatively impact segment-matching performance. Tinchev et al.[[206](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib206)] utilized convolution[[207](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib207)] to obtain an embedding space suitable for urban and natural scenarios. They subsequently estimated match quality through probabilistic geometric validation.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 5.2.2 Classification-based Methods

Several works computed the category of segments by performing classification in the descriptor space. categorized into SegMap[[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208)] family and other methods.

*1) SegMap Family*. As shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(b), the pioneering work SegMap[[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195), [208](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib208)] incrementally clustered point clouds to create a global segment map. It employed segment-wise KNN retrieval with a data-driven descriptor extractor comprising three convolutional and two fully connected layers, then assigned a classification score using a fully connected network. It enabled high compression rates in environment reconstruction and facilitated large-scale 3D LiDAR SLAM. Subsequently, researchers successfully integrated SegMap [[195](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib195)] into LiDAR SLAM[[209](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib209)] and segment-based mapping framework[[210](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib210)].

*2) Other Methods*. Wietrzykowski et al.[[211](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib211)] proposed a DNN that improved segment-based descriptors by learning visual context from synthetic LiDAR intensity images. They claimed that using the latest LiDAR and ambient images could yield additional performance improvements. OneShot[[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib66)] employed a range image-based method[[212](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib212)] for segment extraction and a custom-tailored neural network to extract LiDAR-Vision descriptors.

heading_path: LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey
chunks.text:
#### 5.2.3 Similarity-based Methods

Another approach constructed segment-based descriptors and assessed their similarities, thus combining the advantages of segments and global descriptors. Deep scan context (DSC)[[213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib213)] introduced egocentric segmentation for computing eigenvalues and centroids of segments, employing a GNN to aggregate these features into a descriptor. It outperformed traditional Euclidean clustering in efficiency and robustness for sparse point cloud processing. As shown in Figure [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5 LPR Techniques: Segments ‣ LiDAR-Based Place Recognition For Autonomous Driving: A Survey")(c), Locus [[196](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2306.10561v3#bib.bib196)] encoded topological and temporal information of segments to create a global descriptor using second-order pooling and nonlinear transformation. It avoided global map construction and segment-wise KNN search, achieving robustness to viewpoint changes and occlusions.
